passages.text:
Twelve men follow Odysseus into a cave. Six of them get out.

A giant ate the other six, the one-eyed kind. So where did he come from?

We have four suspects, and a verdict on each. One is an elephant skull. Another, you can still walk up to and touch.

One note before we start. Where Homer gives these characters lines, we have tidied them up. Where he doesn't, we have made a few up. Everything else comes from sources.

But first, a poem. And a very bad decision about cheese.

passages.label: act 1: the stake, the wine, Nobody
passages.text:
Odysseus finds the giant's own club, an olive trunk as big as a ship's mast. He cuts off a length, sharpens it, and hardens the point in the fire.

"Who helps me carry the stake? Draw lots," said Odysseus.

"And if he wakes up?" a crewman asked.

"Then it was a short plan."

He hides the stake under dung, the one thing a cave full of sheep has plenty of.

That evening, two more. Six men gone.

"You have eaten a great deal of man's flesh, Cyclops. Have some wine," said Odysseus, quite calmly.

The wine comes from a priest of Apollo, whose household drank it mixed twenty parts water to one. The giant drinks three bowls. Homer counts.

"More. Now tell me your name, and I will give you a present," the giant rumbled.

"My name is Nobody," said Odysseus.

"Nobody. Then here is my present, Nobody. I will eat Nobody's friends first, and Nobody last."

"I am honoured."

It does buy time.

passages.text:
The giant passes out. Odysseus puts the stake in the fire. Then he puts it in the eye.

Homer reaches for a blacksmith's simile: an axe plunged into cold water, hissing.

"Pollifeemus, what is wrong? Is someone killing you?" a Cyclops asked, bored.

"Nobody is killing me by trickery! Nobody is killing me by force!" the giant bellowed.

"Then nobody is hurting you. It must be a sickness from Zeus. Pray to your father, and let us sleep," the Cyclops said flatly.

The Cyclopes have no laws, no assemblies, and no follow-up questions.

passages.label: act 1: the sheep
passages.text:
At dawn the sheep file out. Odysseus has tied them in threes, with a man hanging under each middle one.

He hangs under the best ram himself. The blinded giant feels along their backs.

Their backs. Not their bellies.

"My good ram. You are always first out. Why are you last today? Are you sorry for your master's eye?" the giant said softly.

The most sincere conversation in the poem.

Odysseus should sail away quietly. He has won.

Instead, he jeers at the giant from the deck. The giant tears the top off a mountain and throws it.

It lands just in front of the ship, a whisker from the rudder, and the wave carries the ship back toward shore.

"A prophet told me Odysseus would take my eye. I expected a warrior. I got a weakling who got me drunk. Come back, and I will give you presents," the giant called.

"Keep your presents. I would send you to Hades if I could. Not even Poseidon will heal that eye."

"Father Poseidon, hear me. Never let Odysseus reach his home. Or if he must, let him come late, in misery, and with all his men lost," the giant prayed.

Ice Age Sicily had elephants, and island life shrank them until the smallest stood under a metre. You could have looked one in the eye.

Their bones have turned up in caves on Sicily and Malta. Head-on, the skull shows two small eye sockets at the sides, and in the middle, one enormous hole.

al. Russia. Even the Arabian Nights.

Most scholars think the tale is older than Homer.

"So I was not the first," Odysseus muttered.

That does not rule out the skull. It does mean the story does not need one.

On that view, Homer did not invent the Cyclops story. He gave us the best-known version.
